William McKinley. The twenty-fifth President of the United States, serving from eighteen ninety-seven until his assassination in nineteen oh-one. A Republican proponent of protective tariffs and American overseas expansion, McKinley presided over the Spanish-American War in eighteen ninety-eight, which resulted in American acquisition of the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico, marking the nation's emergence as an imperial power. His assassination by anarchist Leon Czolgosz elevated Vice President Theodore Roosevelt to the presidency, ushering in the Progressive era.

Born in Ohio, McKinley served as a Union soldier in the Civil War and later as a congressman known for the McKinley Tariff of eighteen ninety, which raised import duties to protect American manufacturers. He was elected president in eighteen ninety-six on a platform of economic nationalism and the protective tariff. His presidency coincided with economic recovery from the eighteen nineties depression, earning him credit for prosperity.

The Spanish-American War, ostensibly fought to liberate Cuba from Spanish rule, lasted only ten weeks and resulted in Spanish cession of the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico to the United States. McKinley's decision to retain the Philippines rather than grant them independence triggered the Philippine-American War from eighteen ninety-nine to nineteen oh-two, a brutal counterinsurgency that killed an estimated two hundred thousand Filipino civilians and soldiers.

McKinley justified American imperial expansion through the ideology of the white man's burden and Christian missions. The Philippines were presented as an opportunity to civilize and Christianize Asian peoples. He was re-elected in nineteen hundred with Theodore Roosevelt as running mate, defeating Democrat William Jennings Bryan's anti-imperialist campaign.

On September sixth, nineteen oh-one, McKinley was assassinated by Leon Czolgosz, an anarchist, while greeting the public at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo. He died eight days later. His death brought Theodore Roosevelt, at age forty-two, to the presidency, transforming American politics and ushering in the Progressive era's more activist executive.
